lines.trans: Wait a minute before you press the light switch, boss.

lines.trans: Why wait? I remember this lamp, look how pretty it is when it lights up!
Mr Mazen, wait, Tariq is holding the screwdriver!
Just one click... pop! Oh dear!
What was that loud noise in the hallway?

Uh-oh, I can hear Salma calling from the dark kitchen!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: أرضية, plural: أرضيين).

examples.trans: The kitchen is on the ground floor.
The ground-floor rooms are close to the courtyard.

meanings.note: Polite Jordanian title for any man ('sir / Mr') as well as 'teacher' or 'professor'.

examples.trans: Please have a seat, sir.
Good morning, gentlemen.

meanings.note: A sigh of dismay or tiredness, a little like English 'oof' or 'ugh'.

examples.trans: Oof, I forgot the key at home!
Ugh, it's hot today.

meanings.note: The typical Jordanian form of شي: في إشي؟ 'is something wrong?', ولا إشي 'nothing at all'.

examples.text: في إشي بدك إياه من السوق؟
examples.trans: Is there anything you want from the market?
Nothing happened at all, relax.

meanings.note: Command to a male to wait.

examples.trans: Wait a moment, I have an idea!
The suitcase is still waiting for its owner.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word for 'want / need', inflected with pronoun suffixes: بدي (I want), بدك (you want), بده (he/it wants), بدها (she/it wants), بدنا (we want), بدكم (you pl. want), بدهم (they want).

examples.trans: I want to read the booking ledger.
Jam bread needs unsalted butter.

meanings.note: Extremely common Jordanian word meaning both 'only / just' (بس نص كاسة 'just half a glass') and 'but' between clauses.

examples.text: بدي أقرأ الدفتر، بس مش ملاقي نظارتي!
examples.trans: I want to read the ledger, only I cannot find my glasses!
Just half a glass, please.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بتذكر, بيتذكر).

examples.trans: Remember your three simple sentences.
I can remember them easily.

meanings.note: The number 9.

examples.trans: The quietness in the courtyard is nine out of ten!
She came back in just nine minutes!

meanings.note: The number 30.

examples.trans: They have given us thirty days in the letter.
The bill is thirty-eight dinars.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: جديدة, plural: جداد).

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I installed a new lightbulb last week.

meanings.note: One of the most frequently used adjectives in Jordanian Arabic to mean beautiful, sweet, nice, or good.

examples.trans: The strawberry jam is sweet and tasty.
The sweater looks lovely and warm.

meanings.note: Transitive, with a doubled middle r (kharrab): someone breaks something. Written the same as خرب; the past خربت is 'I broke' (kharrabt) or 'it broke down' (khirbat) depending on context.

examples.trans: The boy broke the toy on the first day.
Be careful not to break the lock!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: دقايق.

examples.trans: I will be back in ten minutes on the dot.
Wait one minute, please.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: رئيسية, plural: رئيسيين).

examples.trans: We shut off the main water valve in the cellar.
The main gate is on the quiet street.

meanings.note: Placed directly after a noun in Jordanian to mean 'extra' (قطع زيادة extra pieces, الدرج الزيادة the extra stairs).

examples.trans: I brought two extra chairs for the courtyard.
I put a little extra mint in the tea.

meanings.note: Used in the mild exclamation يا ساتر! ('goodness! / heaven forbid!').

examples.trans: Goodness, I nearly dropped the glass!
Goodness, what heavy rain outside!

meanings.note: Active participle of سمع ('to hear'), standard in Jordanian for 'can you hear?' (سامعني؟).

examples.trans: I hear you clearly on the phone.
Do you hear the sound of a car outside the gate?

meanings.note: The number 6.

examples.trans: Room six is on the second floor.
I have six lemons in the basket.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أسلاك.

examples.trans: The old wire needs a slight adjustment.
We checked the bell wire by the door.

meanings.note: Everyday word for a year.

examples.trans: The building is eighty years old.
I have not seen him for three years.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian interrogative pronoun for 'what'.

examples.trans: What is that sound?
What is written on the sheet, Rami?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بصلح, بيصلح).

examples.trans: I fix pipes and chairs.
Yesterday you fixed the old heater.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أصوات.

examples.trans: I heard the sound of rain on the window.
His voice is calm and polite on the phone.

ضرب.gloss: to hit; strike; (of a fuse) blow

meanings.en: to hit; strike; (of a fuse) blow
meanings.note: Basic meaning 'to hit'. In everyday Jordanian a fuse or a machine 'hits' when it blows or fails (الفيوز ضرب 'the fuse blew').

examples.trans: The ball hit the window.

examples.text: الفيوز ضرب لما شغلنا الفرن والغسالة مع بعض.
examples.trans: The fuse blew when we ran the oven and the washing machine together.

meanings.note: Very common Levantine verb meaning to stay, remain, or keep doing something.

examples.trans: Family is what remains.
My teacup stayed intact inside the suitcase!

ضوّى.gloss: to light up; shine; switch on a light

meanings.en: to light up; shine; switch on a light
meanings.note: Used for a lamp that glows and for the person who switches it on (ضوي الضو 'turn on the light').

examples.trans: The new lamp gives good light.
Turn the light on, the room is dark.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: طوابق.

examples.trans: Your room is on the second floor on the right.
The building has three storeys.

meanings.note: A light or fire goes out (الضو طفى 'the light went out'); with a person as subject, to switch something off.

examples.trans: The power went out for a whole hour.
Switch off the light before you sleep.

meanings.note: Sound word for a sharp noise: a click, a pop or a crack.

examples.trans: I heard a pop from the kitchen.
Crack! The glass broke.

meanings.note: Can mean physically high or loud (for a voice or sound).

examples.trans: What is that loud sound upstairs?
The wooden ceiling is high and sunny.

meanings.note: Arabic expresses age with عمر + possessive suffix: عمره تمانين سنة ('its/his age is eighty years').

examples.trans: The building is eighty years old.
He has lived in this quarter all his life.

meanings.note: A very common preposition used to indicate location, possession, or presence.

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door.
I have a reservation under the name Suad.

meanings.note: The main meal of the day in Jordan, usually eaten in the early afternoon.

examples.trans: What's for lunch today?
We have lunch together after work.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for a room in a house or building.

examples.trans: We have eight comfortable rooms at the guesthouse.
Room four is ready and clean.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بفحص, بيفحص).

examples.trans: Tariq will inspect the cellar right away.
We checked the heater and pipes this morning.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أفران.

examples.text: لفائف القرفة طلعت من الفرن هلا.
examples.trans: The cinnamon rolls just came out of the oven.
The bakery down the street bakes in the morning.

meanings.note: Loanword from English 'fuse'; when one blows, people say الفيوز ضرب.

examples.trans: I changed the fuse and the light came back.
The fuse box is next to the door.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقول, بيقول).

examples.trans: What does clause fourteen say?
He said thank you and hung up!

meanings.note: Preposition and adverb for time or sequence meaning 'prior to' or 'before'.

examples.text: علمت بيانو هون قبل خمسة وعشرين سنة.
examples.trans: I taught piano here twenty-five years ago.
Drink your coffee before the rush.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقدر, بيقدر).

examples.text: بنقدر نقدم زبدة مالحة مع المربى؟
examples.trans: Can we serve salted butter with jam?

examples.text: ليش ما قدرت تعطيه القطار بإيدك؟
examples.trans: Why could you not hand him the train yourself?

meanings.note: The primary interrogative word for quantity, price, or duration in Levantine Arabic.

examples.trans: What time is it right now?
Look how peaceful the sky is!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: قديمة, plural: قدام).

examples.trans: The courtyard has an old jasmine tree.
The old hardware shop is past the bridge.

meanings.note: Any fabric; سلك قماش is old cloth-covered electrical wire.

examples.trans: She bought blue fabric for the curtains.
This fabric is very soft.

meanings.note: The Amman verb for pressing a button, doorbell or switch.

examples.text: اكبس الزر الأحمر عشان يفتح الباب.
examples.trans: Press the red button to open the door.

examples.text: كبست الجرس مرتين وما حدا فتح.
examples.trans: I pressed the bell twice and nobody opened.

كبسة.gloss: a press; a click (of a button)

meanings.en: a press; a click (of a button)
meanings.note: One press of a button: بكبسة وحدة 'with one click'.

examples.trans: With one press the machine starts.
Two presses on the bell means it is me.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: كشافات.

examples.trans: Hold the flashlight steady on the pipe joint.
The flashlight beam is bright and clear in the basement.

meanings.note: Indispensable Levantine and Egyptian particle meaning 'also', 'too', or 'as well'.

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: Spoken form of كهرباء; الكهربا قطعت 'the power is cut'.

examples.trans: The power came back after an hour.
The electricity bill is expensive this month.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'no' or 'not', used exactly like Standard Arabic.

examples.trans: No, lift the handle first.
Do not worry, ma'am.

meanings.note: Common conjunction used to introduce a time clause, distinct from the question word 'when' (mita).

examples.trans: Smile when the bell rings!
When I get nervous, my sentences turn long.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: لمبات.

examples.trans: I fitted a new bulb in the attic bathroom.
The white lightbulb is bright.

meanings.note: The standard colloquial interrogative for 'why' in Jordanian Arabic.

examples.trans: Why did the person run off without his bag?
Why do you keep looking at the clock?

meanings.note: Used mostly as a negative particle for verbs ('didn't') or as a relative pronoun/conjunction ('what' or 'that which').

examples.trans: Paper does not lose room names.
Have tea before you head out.

meanings.note: Active participle indicating the ongoing state of gripping or grasping something.

examples.trans: I am holding the torch steady!
He was holding a blue suitcase in his hand.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مداخل.

examples.trans: The guesthouse entrance is lit by a brass lantern.
We greeted the guests at the entrance.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بمسك, بيمسك).

examples.trans: Hold this torch steady right here.
Grab the boxes, Tariq!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مطابخ.

examples.trans: The smell of bread is coming from the kitchen.
The guesthouse kitchen is spacious and clean.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: معتمة, plural: معتمين).

examples.trans: The entrance was dim during the rain.
We lit the lanterns because the hallway is dim.

meanings.note: In Jordanian speech, يا معلم is an affectionate, respectful way to address a boss or skilled craftsperson.

examples.trans: You are all generosity, boss!
She was a very gifted piano teacher.

meanings.note: Means both a door key and a mechanic's spanner/wrench (مفتاح حديد iron wrench).

examples.trans: Here is the key to room four.
We have eight brass keys on the board.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مفكات.

examples.trans: He always carries a small screwdriver in his pocket.
Pass me the screwdriver from the toolbox.

meanings.note: An inside hallway or a narrow passage between buildings.

examples.trans: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.
The hallway is dark, turn on the light.

meanings.note: One of the most basic Arabic prepositions indicating origin.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'good' and adverbially 'well' (نمت منيح؟ 'did you sleep well?').

examples.trans: It has a good, comfortable wooden bed.
Did you sleep well under the wooden ceiling?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بنادي, بينادي).

examples.trans: Do we call each other by first name here?
Salma called everyone to breakfast.

meanings.note: Used for the metal or objects made of it.

examples.trans: We polished the brass keys in the morning.
The brass pot is old and engraved.

meanings.note: Everyday demonstrative pronoun for masculine singular objects.

examples.trans: Here we use this big ledger.
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: Cardinal number or used as an indefinite pronoun.

examples.trans: Not a single scratch on the cup!
The gate rang with one strong ring.

meanings.note: Vocative particle used when addressing someone directly.

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Standard noun for day, often used in expressions like 'el-yom' (today).

examples.trans: Today the weather is sunny and warm in Amman.
Have a happy, successful day!
